newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian stocks close broadly down on U.S. fall.
newsitem.headline: Australian stocks close broadly down on U.S. fall.

text.p: The Australian share market slowly moved away from its early lows to close 1.8 percent down on Monday as investors nervously awaited the next U.S. session after Friday's 3.1 percent dive on Wall Street.
The All Ordinaries index ended 47.7 points lower at 2,618.5 after hitting an early low of 2,589.8.
Turnover was a moderate A$715 million (US$529 million).
"Certainly, if we get U.S. market weakness it will inevitably flow through to the domestic market," said David Lansley, senior treasury economist at National Australia Bank.
"It's hard to know if we are seeing a real correction though. I guess the thing that really concerns us is the outlook for U.S. corporate earnings," Lansley said.
The Australian share market has lost around 5.3 percent since its record high 2,727.9 on July 8, while Wall Street has fallen 6.8 percent from the August 6 high of 8,259.
Dealers said players would also keep a cautious eye on Tuesday's U.S. Federal Reserve meeting, although no change to monetary policy is expected.
Domestically, the accelerating reporting season could give investors further clues on where prices are heading.
"What we've seen so far has been rather flat, but this reflects the past. The interesting thing will be to see what the forecasts are," one equity strategist said.
News Corp, John Fairfax and Normandy Mining are among those releasing annual results this week.

News Corp closed three cents lower at A$5.92 ahead of Wednesday's report, expected to show a 12 percent increase in net profit before abnormal items to around A$1.42 billion compared to A$1.263 billion in 1995/96. Newspaper publisher Fairfax was steady at A$3.19 pending Tuesday's figures.
Fairfax is seen revealing a net profit before abnormals of A$90.3 million compared to A$102 million in the 1995/96 year.
Normandy closed unchanged at A$1.61. Analysts said the miner was expected to post a healthy profit increase to around A$120 million for the year to June 30.
Nickel producer QNI finished seven cents lower at A$2.11 after reporting a net profit fall to A$32.11 million in 1996/97 from A$85.89 million a year ago.
Bellwether BHP ended 39.2 cents lower at A$17.108.
"You could argue that the price of copper rather than the market generally has caused BHP to fall, together with the problems it has had recently," said Kevin Lourey of broker Peake Lands Kirwan.
Two other major miners also fell more than the overall market. WMC fell 19.1 cents to A$7.28, while Rio Tinto closed 50 cents lower at A$20.98.
Commonwealth Bank shares worth nearly A$115 million were traded as the stock went ex-dividend by 57 cents. The bank ended 75.4 cents lower at A$15.84.
Lend Lease also gained ground, up eight cents to A$28.40.

The company said on Sunday its project management and funds management units would post 40 percent higher revenues in the current year. "It's a growth stock and their full-year result was good," one Sydney-based dealer said.
The retail sector was the weakest with a three percent drop as profit-taking added to the general weak sentiment.
Coles Myer fell 27 cents to A$6.33 and Woolworths 10 cents to A$4.10 after a good run on Friday.
